newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria calm on anniversary of annulled vote.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria calm on anniversary of annulled vote.

text.p: Nigeria was quiet on Thursday on the fourth anniversary of an annulled presidential poll, but the crisis triggered by the action still remained visible.
Police display of firepower and warnings against protests ensured there were no demonstrations.
Even well-advertised rallies planned by a pro-government group were cancelled, despite their aim of urging military ruler General Sani Abacha to stand in next year's presidential poll.
"There is no report of disturbances anywhere," said a police spokesman in Lagos, the hotbed of opposition to Abacha's rule.
"Everywhere is calm and quiet," he added.

But across Africa's most populous nation, problems of everyday living were visible and remained a potent reminder that the multi-ethnic nation has yet to recover from the annulment of the "June 12" presidential vote as the event has come to be known.
"This nation has not been united since the annulment and that is why nothing is working," said banker Gbenga Oluwa.
Long queues for petrol caused by recurring fuel shortages in Africa's leading oil-producing nation are seen in many cities.
Unemployment remains high with thousands of qualified youths roaming the streets with no jobs.
"I would probably have been in a cosy job if June 12 had been allowed and Nigeria had become a democracy," said Bola Kuye, a 1993 university graduate still without employment.
Millionaire businessman Moshood Abiola was coasting to victory in the poll to end 10 straight years of army rule when the then ruler General Ibrahim Babangida scrapped the poll.
Nigeria plunged into turmoil with street riots, especially in the southwest which includes Lagos, Abiola's home region.

Local newspapers said Babangida's hilltop retirement home in Minna, central Nigeria had been cordoned off by police since Wednesday following threats by students to march on it to protest over the election annulment.

Since the annulment, Nigeria has been shunned by the West and many other powerful nations for lack of democracy and alleged human rights abuses and this has in turn curtailed foreign investment with consequences for the economy and jobs.

Abacha, an infantry general who seized power in the turmoil of 1993 is implementing a programme to hand over power next year but the opposition says his hidden ambition is to transform himself into an elected leader.

They cite the continued detention of several opposition figures and of Abiola, who has been held since he declared himself president in June 1994, as evidence that Abacha is not interested in reconciliation to make his transition successful.

Multi-ethnic Nigeria remains divided over June 12. The north where Abacha comes from generally backs him while Abiola's southwestern region wants the election validated, and the east which was at the receiving end of the Biafra civil war is neutral.
"June 12 will make or mar this country...but it is not too late in the day to sit down and resolve this crisis," said Lagos human rights activist Femi Falana, an Abiola supporter.
Nigerian newspaper editorials on the day echoed that sentiment, urging Abacha to free Abiola from detention and to negotiate with him in order to restore lasting peace in Nigeria.

"It is in the overall interest of the nation that Chief Abiola and other prisoners of conscience be first released," wrote the independent National Concord, adding "Then a means of dialogue can be established...A transition programme without this start-off point of justice and fair play is doomed to fail."
